transcript.text: Samsung WD90T534DBW washer dryer - clothes are still damp at the end of the wash and dry programme. It's not that old. Is the heater going?

Not necessarily. Damp clothes at the end of a washer-dryer cycle are more often caused by too much in the dry load, a short/low drying setting, or a restriction in the condensation/drain path than by the heater. The key distinction is heat: 1. During the drying stage, carefully open the door only once the programme permits it, or feel the laundry as soon as it ends. If it is clearly warm/hot but still damp, the heater is working. Suspect an oversized dry load, the selected drying level, or a fluff/condensation/drainage restriction. 2. If the drum turns but the laundry remains completely cold throughout a drying programme, a drying heater, thermostat or thermal cut-out becomes more likely and would normally need an engineer. 3. Check the load against the stated dry capacity, not the wash capacity. A washer-dryer typically dries substantially less than it can wash; a full wash load left in for drying commonly finishes damp. Try a smaller load on a full drying programme/high dryness setting. 4. Make sure the cold-water tap is on and the inlet and drain hoses are not kinked. These machines generally use cold water to condense moisture during drying and pump that water away. If the load was modest and properly spun beforehand, and it stays cold on a full drying programme, stop there and arrange a repair rather than assuming it is just a setting.
Clothes come out hot but damp, so the heater seems to be working. I do put a full 9kg drum in and do the wash and dry in one go, if that matters.

Yes — that very likely matters. A 9 kg figure is the wash capacity, not the drying capacity. A washer-dryer can wash a full drum but normally has to dry a substantially smaller load. With the whole wash left in, it can get the clothes hot yet leave them damp simply because moisture cannot be removed quickly enough. That makes a failed heater unlikely. 1. Check the rating label or manual for the separate drying capacity, then split the washed load into batches no larger than that figure. Use a full drying programme or high dryness level. If the smaller batch dries properly, there is no fault: it is normal capacity limitation.
2. Keep the cold-water tap fully on and check the inlet and drain hoses behind the machine are not kinked or squashed. Washer-dryers use water during drying to condense moisture and must pump it away.
3. If a smaller load is still hot but remains damp, switch off and unplug it, put towels and a shallow tray at the lower front, then clean the pump filter slowly. Fluff/debris there can restrict drainage during drying.
The manual says 6kg for drying, so I'm over that. I tried a half drum with full spin and it came out dry. I do often turn the spin down to 800 though, does that matter?

Yes, it matters. An 800 rpm spin leaves noticeably more water in the clothes than a higher spin, so the dryer has much more moisture to remove. Combined with putting more than the 6 kg drying limit in, that explains hot but damp laundry. For reliable wash-and-dry results: keep the load at or below 6 kg for drying, and use the highest spin speed the fabric care labels allow. For a full 9 kg wash, remove roughly a third to half of it before drying, or run an extra high-spin cycle and dry in batches.

candidates: Dry load too large or drying programme/level not sufficient (high)
Restricted condensation, drainage or fluff path during drying (medium)
Drying heater, thermostat or thermal cut-out fault (low)
